items.title: Withdraw conformance and benchmark claims sitewide; decouple site build from wasm
items.body:
## TLDR

Withdraws Basilisk's 100% conformance claim and its published benchmark figures across the whole public site (English and Chinese), replaces them with a linked correction and the integrity audit that explains why, and decouples the Eleventy build from the Rust wasm build so a non-compiling checker can no longer take the entire site down.

## What Was Added?

- **`docs/CONFORMANCE-INTEGRITY-AUDIT.md`** (285 lines) — the record of what was found: checker logic fitted to the exact contents of conformance fixtures rather than implementing the typing specification generally, including a type-alias validator matching prefixes and substrings of raw source text with a special case for `eval(` because that spelling appeared in one test file.
- **Explicit `Build playground engine (wasm)` step** in both `ci.yml`'s website job and `deploy-pages.yml`, replacing the implicit one that `npm run build` used to chain.
- **`.bench-caveat` notice** on `/docs/benchmarks/`, stating the figures are withdrawn pending an integrity review and must not be used to compare Basilisk with other tools.
- New e2e assertions that the old claims are *absent*: `expect(body).not.toContain("scores 100%")` and `expect(body).not.toContain("fastest we've benchmarked")`.

## What Was Changed or Deleted?

- **Homepage (EN + ZH)** — headline drops "the only Python type checker that scores 100% … and the fastest we've benchmarked" for "An open-source Python type checker and language server, built in Rust." The two hero proof cards now read *Current typing conformance* and *Published benchmark figures*, both pointing at the withdrawal.
- **`/docs/conformance/`** — retitled "Basilisk Conformance Results Are Withdrawn"; the leaderboard table, the "How it's measured" section and the reproduce-it-yourself instructions are removed. States plainly that Basilisk was removed from the `python/typing` results table at our request and that its current percentage is temporarily unknown.
- **`_data/conformanceOfficial.js`** — no longer exports live claim data (`basiliskRank`, `perfectCount`, `basiliskIsSolePerfect`). It now exports `withdrawn: true`, `publicationStatus: "historical-withdrawn"`, and nests the frozen snapshot under `historical.*` with `basiliskWasSolePerfectAtSnapshot`. `resultsDir` is repointed from `main` to the pinned commit so the snapshot cannot silently re-render as current.
- **`website/package.json`** — `"build"` changes from `npm run build:wasm && eleventy` to `eleventy`. Every page but the playground renders from committed data, so the site build no longer has a Rust dependency.
- **Site/social metadata** — `eleventy.config.js` description, `package.json` description, `site.json`, og-image, banner SVG/PNGs and the `og:title` all updated; page title drops "Fast".
- **Blog posts (EN + ZH)** — the 100%-conformance announcement and five other posts updated so no retracted claim survives in an older article.
- **`/docs/comparison.md`**, `/docs/index.md`, `quick-start`, `migration`, `install-vscode`, `releases.njk`, `benchmark-section.njk`, `conformance-chart.njk` — comparative claims removed or re-scoped.

## How Do The Automated Tests Prove It Works?

`npm run test:e2e` — **52 passed, 6 skipped, 0 failed** on both the `desktop` (Desktop Chrome) and `mobile` (iPhone SE, 375×667) projects, run with `CI=1` so `reuseExistingServer` is off exactly as in CI.

The suite proves the correction is actually rendered, not just committed:

- `homepage.spec.ts` › *puts the integrity correction beside the product introduction* — asserts the subheadline contains "withdrawn both our former conformance claim and our published benchmark figures", "removed from the official python/typing results at our request", "current conformance percentage is temporarily unknown", and "robustness and mutation testing".
- `homepage.spec.ts` › *shows both withdrawn result notices and their detail links* — asserts exactly 2 stat cards, "removed from the official results table", "Both sets of figures are withdrawn", **and that the body no longer contains "scores 100%" or "fastest we've benchmarked"**. This is the assertion that fails if a retracted claim is reintroduced anywhere on the page.
- `homepage.spec.ts` › *Chinese homepage › renders the same correction and withdrawn-result notices* — the same gates in `zh`, so one locale cannot quietly keep a claim the other withdrew, plus *keeps its disclosure structure aligned with the English page*.
- `benchmarks.spec.ts` — asserts `.bench-caveat` contains "benchmark figures are withdrawn pending an integrity review" and "Do not use the values below to compare Basilisk with other tools".
- `playground.spec.ts` (4 tests × 2 viewports) — drives the real wasm engine, proving the `npm run build` decoupling did not break the playground.

Also run locally and green: `python3 scripts/gen_rules_reference.py --data` + `diff` (rules.json in sync, 169 codes), `python3 scripts/gen_conformance_reference.py --check` (stamped references and generated READMEs in sync), `npm run build:wasm` under CI's `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings -C link-arg=-zstack-size=16777216"`, `npm run build` (302 files), `cargo fmt --all --check` (0 diffs) and `cargo check --workspace --all-targets`.

`make ci` (`lint test build`) was not run in full: this branch changes no Rust, and CI path-filters those jobs off for it (`code=false`). `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` and `cargo fmt --all --check` both pass.

## Spec / Doc Changes

- `docs/CONFORMANCE-INTEGRITY-AUDIT.md` — new; linked from the site's conformance correction.
- `docs/INDEX.md` — registers the audit under a new *Conformance integrity* section.
- `docs/specs/WASM-SPEC.md` — records that the playground engine is built by an explicit `build:wasm` step, separate from the Eleventy build.
- `docs/specs/WEBSITE-E2E-SPEC.md` — `[WEBSITE-E2E-SMOKE]` rewritten: the homepage gates now assert the integrity disclosures and the absence of the withdrawn claims, in both locales.

## Breaking Changes

- [x] None to any shipped binary or API. `_data/conformanceOfficial.js` changes shape (live fields replaced by `withdrawn` + `historical.*`), which is internal to the site build and consumed only by templates updated in this PR.

Refs #379, #408

items.title: Gate the facts docs/index.html and docs/index.md both state
items.body: ## The blind spot `docs/index.md` is the Markdown companion agents fetch via `rel="alternate"` and `llms.txt` — an LLM asking about Vera's benchmark results is served that file, not the landing page. It is not derived from `docs/index.html`. It is written out by `build_index_md()` in `scripts/build_site.py`, which holds the landing page's substance as a hand-maintained f-string. `scripts/check_site_assets.py` verified it by calling that generator and comparing the result against the committed file. Both sides of that comparison come from the same function, so a generator that missed an edit to the hand-designed HTML produced a committed asset stale in exactly the same way, and the check was satisfied. The gate proved the asset matched the generator; nothing proved the generator matched the HTML it mirrors. A v0.0.7-era benchmark section survived every intervening release until it was caught by hand. This is option 2 from the issue: keep the generator, gate the pair. It extends `check_site_assets.py` rather than adding a script — this is that script's documented blind spot, and it inherits the existing CI wiring (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, lint job). No new CI job or pre-commit entry. ## Facts gated `check_fact_coherence(html_path, md_path)` extracts each fact from both files independently and compares: | Fact | Where | |---|---| | VeraBench version | `VeraBench v0.0.18` in both | | Tested Vera version | `Vera v0.1.8` in both | | Landing-page version badge | HTML `v0.1.8`, MD `**Current version:** [0.1.8]` | | Benchmark problem count | `A 60-problem benchmark` | | Benchmark difficulty tiers | `across 5 difficulty tiers` | | Benchmark model count | `Nine models, three providers` | | Benchmark provider count | same sentence | | Models writing perfect Vera | `Six of nine frontier models` | | Results table | 9 rows; per row the model name, tier and all three figures (Vera / Python / TypeScript) | | Rows vs stated model count | each file's table row count against its own prose | | Editor names | VS Code, Vim, TextMate | Compared as facts, not wording: number words fold onto digits (`Nine` = `9`), HTML entities and tags are stripped from table cells, Markdown emphasis is stripped (`**100%**` = `100%` — the win/loss marking is the presentational equivalent of the HTML's CSS class), and percentages compare as strings. The two files' prose registers are left alone. `check_version_sync.py` is not duplicated: it pins the HTML badge to `pyproject.toml` and never reads `docs/index.md`. The new check compares the two documents to each other. **Extraction failure is gate failure.** If a fact cannot be located in either file, that is an error naming the fact and the file — a reworded sentence must not be able to switch its own check off. A file stating one fact two different ways is also an error. An example failure, from a deliberately drifted `docs/index.html`: ``` ERROR: 2 landing-page fact(s) diverge between docs/index.html and docs/index.md (fix build_index_md() in scripts/build_site.py): VeraBench version differs: …/docs/index.html says '0.0.19', …/docs/index.md says '0.0.18' benchmark table row 'Claude Fable 5' differs: …/docs/index.html says (tier=ceiling, Vera=42%, Python=97%, TypeScript=97%), …/docs/index.md says (tier=ceiling, Vera=100%, Python=97%, TypeScript=97%) ``` ## RED-first evidence 19 tests were written in `tests/test_build_site.py` before `check_fact_coherence` existed, and all 19 failed. Each drift case copies the committed pair into `tmp_path` and mutates the copy — the real files are never touched — and the mutation helper asserts its anchor is unique, so a reworded landing page turns the test red rather than silently no-op'ing. Proved to fail: a bumped percentage in the HTML table, and in the Markdown table; a bumped VeraBench version; a bumped tested-Vera version; a diverged version badge; a changed problem count; a changed model count (which also trips the rows-vs-prose cross-check); a removed HTML table row, and a removed Markdown row; a renamed model; a changed tier; a dropped editor. Extraction failures proved to fail: a removed HTML ``, a removed Markdown table header, a deleted results caveat (both facts on that line named), a removed editor claim, a missing file, and one file stating the VeraBench version two different ways. Then mutation-validated: six extraction regexes were broken one at a time — the HTML row extractor, the HTML table anchor, the VeraBench version pattern, the Markdown table header, the Vim editor pattern, the Markdown emphasis stripper — and each turned at least one test red. None is dead weight. The committed `docs/index.html` / `docs/index.md` pair passes: all 9 table rows match cell for cell, all 8 prose facts agree, and all three editors are named in both. No existing divergence was found. Full gate green: `pytest tests/` (8,471 passed), `check_site_assets.py`, `check_doc_counts.py`, `check_explicit_encoding.py`, `check_version_sync.py`, `ruff check .`, `ruff check --select S vera/`, `mypy vera/`. ## Docs lockstep CHANGELOG `[Unreleased]` gains a `### Fixed` entry; the `#1154` row is removed from `KNOWN_ISSUES.md` (no matching row existed in `SKILL.md`); `CLAUDE.md` and `TESTING.md` describe what the script now checks; `CONTRIBUTING.md` says plainly that `docs/index.md` has to be edited in `build_index_md()` alongside the HTML. The `TESTING.md` / `README.md` / `ROADMAP.md` test counts move with the 19 new tests. Closes #1154 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **Bug Fixes** - Added checks to detect missing, malformed, or conflicting facts between the HTML and Markdown landing pages. - Site validation now reports detailed discrepancies and fails when the pages are inconsistent. - **Documentation** - Updated guidance for maintaining both landing-page formats. - Removed the related known issue. - Updated the documented project test count to 8,589. - **Tests** - Added comprehensive coverage for landing-page consistency checks and failure scenarios.

items.title: docs: add bench/ and docs/evaluations/, with the ICDAR 2013 result
items.body:
Benchmark harnesses and measurement findings had no home. The ICDAR 2013 harness was living in a temp directory, and every result from this work existed only in Linear — which records that something was *decided*, not what was *measured*.

## What this adds

```
bench/                          separate Go module
  README.md
  icdar2013/
    run.py                      fetch dataset, build, score
    extract.go                  dumps pdftable's tables as JSON
    score.py                    adjacency-relation metric
    diag.py                     detection vs structure breakdown
docs/
  README.md
  evaluations/
    2026-08-02-icdar2013-table-structure.md
    2026-08-02-font-metrics-and-table-fidelity.md
```

## `bench/` is a separate Go module, deliberately

Nested modules are excluded from the parent's `./...`, so the library build ignores it and a consumer of `pdftable` never fetches its dependencies.

**The first version of this commit got that wrong** — `go list ./...` showed `github.com/hallelx2/pdftable/bench/icdar2013` inside the library module, which is precisely the leak the split exists to prevent. Fixed and verified:

```
$ go list ./...
github.com/hallelx2/pdftable
github.com/hallelx2/pdftable/cmd/pdftable
github.com/hallelx2/pdftable/examples/extract_tables
github.com/hallelx2/pdftable/internal/layout
github.com/hallelx2/pdftable/internal/pdf
```

Datasets are not committed. `run.py` fetches ICDAR 2013 (~12 MB) into a cache dir, builds the extractor as its own module against the working tree, and scores pdftable **alongside pdfplumber** — "is 0.36 good?" is unanswerable without a baseline.

## `docs/evaluations/` — dated, append-only

Each report states the commit it ran against, the external oracle used, the metric precisely, **what the number is not comparable to**, and **what remains untested**.

That last part is the point. A benchmark number without its scope reads as a general claim. The 0.362 here is *end-to-end detection plus structure* — not the structure-only task that papers report 0.85–0.95 on, where the system is handed the table region.

Append-only means a regression appears as a diff between two dated files rather than vanishing into a rewrite.

## What did NOT move, and why

The library source stays in the repository root. For a single-package Go library the root **is** the import path — moving `page.go` into `src/` or `pkg/` breaks every consumer, and `pkg/` is a recognised Go anti-pattern. Go also deliberately keeps `_test.go` beside the code it covers.

The README now documents the layout, so the root is legible rather than merely conventional.

## Verification

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./... -count=1 -race` — green.
- `bench/` confirmed absent from `go list ./...`.
- Harness re-run from its new home; results reproduce.

Relates to HAL-568

## Summary

Two research deliverables for the issues assigned to me.

Closes #187. Addresses #99 as far as it can go while #100 is open.

## #187 — `docs/research/encrypted-byo-storage-sync.md`

Compares local export, filesystem/NAS targets, generic S3-compatible storage, and consumer drive providers on privacy, portability, cost, offline behaviour, and maintenance. Recommends a v1 boundary of **manual, encrypted, resumable snapshots to an S3-compatible endpoint or a filesystem path**, behind a `SyncTarget` interface kept deliberately separate from the live `StorageBackend`.

Two findings from the code shaped the design:

- The provider-neutral storage abstraction **has already landed** (`storage_abstract.py`, `storage_factory.py`, …), so the ADR's "not started" status line is stale.
- **The vault no longer encrypts media at rest.** Per the vault design note, 1.1.3 keeps hidden media in the ordinary private store behind password-gated sessions and migrates legacy AES-GCM blobs back to plaintext. It is an access-control boundary, not a cryptographic one — so the requirement that "vault blobs are encrypted locally before upload" **cannot be met by reusing vault behaviour**. Sync must own its own encryption layer.

Consumer drive providers are deferred with reasons: OAuth puts a Find-registered client identity in the trust path, which weakens the local-first promise beyond the engineering cost. Users wanting Drive/Dropbox can point the filesystem target at a provider-synced folder or an `rclone mount` — covers the case in v1 with zero provider code.

## #99 — `docs/research/search-retrieval-benchmark-plan.md`

#99 is blocked on #100 and says explicitly not to start comparisons until one labeled dataset can evaluate every candidate. So this adds everything that does **not** depend on the harness — baseline audit, candidate matrix, measurement protocol, adoption gates, rollback boundaries — and stops where real data is required. **No relevance numbers are included, deliberately.** When #100 lands the results table fills in without redesigning anything.

The baseline audit found three drifted assumptions, one of them material:

> An HNSW index has landed (`ix_media_vector_hnsw`) and search does `ORDER BY vector <=> … LIMIT`, so Find is very likely **already serving approximate results** — while `vector-search-benchmarks.md` still frames exact scan as "current default" and states recall is "perfect by definition". The index uses **default build parameters** and **`hnsw.ef_search` is never set anywhere** in the codebase.

Measuring deployed recall against exact search is therefore the highest-value single measurement available, and it is sequenced first — it may surface a live quality regression that predates #99.

Also corrects the record that reranking is *partial* rather than absent (`search_ranking.py` exists), and that latency instrumentation is already in place.

Docs only, no code changes. Every cited file path and quoted status line was verified against the tree on this branch.

Generates real discrimination/calibration evidence for the scores against a
labeled cohort. Since no real cohort is available (data/ is gitignored and was
removed), this uses a seeded, fully reproducible synthetic cohort — a *functional*
validation of the engine, clearly NOT clinical evidence.

- services/synthetic_cohort.py: seeded cohort with a transparent multi-organ DGP.
  Mortality is driven by total organ-failure burden + age (independent of any
  score's output — no circularity), so multi-organ scores should lead as they do
  clinically.
- validate_scores.py: runs every score over the cohort, computes AUROC (in each
  score's risk direction) and SAPS II calibration, writes the report. Swap
  load_cohort() for a real cohort to produce clinical evidence.
- services/clinical_scores.py: RISK_DIRECTION as the single source of truth for
  each score's risk orientation.
- tests/test_synthetic_validation.py: determinism + AUROC thresholds (multi-organ
  scores lead; all discriminate). 128 tests, 97% coverage on the clinical modules.

Results (docs/VALIDATION_RESULTS.md + results/tables/score_validation.csv):
every score discriminates (AUROC ~0.67-0.81); SOFA/APACHE II/SAPS II/NEWS2 lead;
the harness also detects SAPS II miscalibration (under-prediction) — illustrating
why local recalibration matters. VALIDATION.md updated to reference it.

items.body:
Related to #1960 — adds the ViT benchmark requested in [this maintainer comment](https://github.com/lightly-ai/lightly/issues/1960#issuecomment-5056968762), building on the `VISRegLoss` from #1968.

## Description
- [ ] My change is breaking

Registers VISReg as a selectable method in the `imagenet/vitb16` runner: a new `benchmarks/imagenet/vitb16/visreg.py` (VISReg `LightningModule` + multi-crop `transform`) plus a two-line entry in `main.py`'s `METHODS` dict. The module mirrors `lejepa.py` so the two run head-to-head on the same backbone, optimizer, and eval, differing only where VISReg's paper says they should.

Per the maintainer note ("use the best setting in the paper as much as possible, like LeJEPA"), the settings are VISReg's own paper-best, each cross-checked against the paper **and** the official repo (not just the paper prose, which diverges from the code in two places):

| Setting | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| backbone | `vit_small_patch16_224` | ViT-S/16 — smaller than the paper's ViT-B/16 per the maintainer ("we train smaller models") |
| views | 4 global + 6 local | paper App. A.1 / repo `n_global: 4` (needs a custom `MultiViewTransform`; `DINOTransform` is fixed at 2 global) |
| augmentation | one uniform recipe on every crop (blur 0.5, solarize 0.2) | reference `_shared_aug` |
| lr | `9e-4` | paper Table 3 (9e-4 > 5e-4 at this scale); repo `lr: 9e-4` |
| projector | 3-layer MLP `embed→2048→2048→256`, BatchNorm + **GELU**, last layer bare | reference `ViTEncoder.proj` (`proj_gelu: true`); projects the **last-layer** CLS only |
| loss | `VISRegLoss(num_slices=2048, gather_distributed=True)` | K per paper App. A.1; `gather_distributed=True` matches the reference's autograd-aware `all_gather` before the reg statistics, and the sibling LeJEPA |
| λ / weight decay | `0.9` / `5e-2` | paper + repo |

Two spots where the reference code overrides the paper's own text, worth noting since they look like bugs otherwise: the projector runs on the **last-layer CLS token only** (`self.proj(last_cls)`), not the "concatenated last-two-layer CLS" the paper describes — that concat is the eval-probe embedding — so `input_dim=embed_dim`, not `2×`; and the augmentation is a single distribution shared by all crops, with no DINO-style global asymmetry.

Purely additive: no `lightly/` source is touched, `VISRegLoss` is only imported, and the new `METHODS["visreg"]` key affects a run only when `--methods visreg` is passed.

## Tests
- [ ] My change is covered by existing tests.
- [ ] My change needs new tests.
- [ ] I have added/adapted the tests accordingly.
- [x] I have manually tested the change.

Benchmark method modules aren't unit-tested in this repo (same as `dino.py`, `lejepa.py`, etc.) and sit outside the `pytest`/`mypy` targets, so I verified with a smoke test plus the standard checks. **Before:** `--methods visreg` is not a registered method. **After:** it constructs and trains a step end-to-end.

# smoke test: transform emits 4 global + 6 local, projector is the paper's GELU
# 384->2048->2048->256, and one training step runs end-to-end
python - <<'PY'
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "benchmarks/imagenet/vitb16")
import torch, visreg
from PIL import Image
v = visreg.transform(Image.new("RGB", (256, 256)))
print(len(v), "views;", sum(x.shape[-1] == 224 for x in v), "global,", sum(x.shape[-1] == 96 for x in v), "local")
m = visreg.VISReg(batch_size_per_device=4, num_classes=10)
m.log = m.log_dict = lambda *a, **k: None
b = [torch.randn(4, 3, 224, 224)] * 4 + [torch.randn(4, 3, 96, 96)] * 6
print("loss", float(m.training_step((b, torch.randint(0, 10, (4,)), [""] * 4), 0).detach()))
PY
# -> 10 views; 4 global, 6 local
# -> loss ~3 (finite scalar; exact value varies with random init)

ruff check benchmarks/imagenet/vitb16/visreg.py benchmarks/imagenet/vitb16/main.py   # All checks passed!
```

The full ImageNet run (ViT-S/16, `--methods visreg`) that produces the comparison numbers + checkpoint is left to the maintainers' cluster.

Gives the project the two-regime structure the satellite track (#192) has needed since #214: the ISL suite existed as CI gates and an example binary, but had **no view** (the benchmarks index presented MANET as the only regime) and **no dispatchable benchmark** (nothing ran `isl-grid` outside second-scale CI smokes).

**One build, two views.** This deliberately does *not* fork the protocol or the images — ADR-0015 decided that and nothing here reopens it. What splits is presentation and instrumentation: which harness, which baselines, which gates, which results pages.

| | MANET (original) | Satellite (ISL) |
|---|---|---|
| harness | `anthocnet-compare` (wifi field) | `isl-grid` (+Grid torus, p2p ISLs, one interface per link) |
| suite entry | `docs/benchmarks.md` | `docs/benchmarks/satellite/isl-grid.md` (new) |
| dispatch | `paper-benchmark.yml` / `scenario-matrix.yml` | **`satellite-benchmark.yml` (new)** |
| per-PR gates | anchors + determinism (literature-derived) | anchors + determinism (**analytic** — stricter, #237/#238) |
| results | per-merge refresh + committed campaigns | manual dispatch; **none committed yet, by design** |

## `satellite-benchmark.yml`

Mirror of `paper-benchmark.yml` for the grid's own knobs (`rows/cols/torus/islDelayMs/islRate/flows/cbrBps/runs/protocols/extraArgs`), inheriting its hardening **by construction**: bash+pipefail+captured stderr (#28 — a bad `extraArgs` must fail the job, not pass with an empty table), explicit build-profile resolution (#123), `/usr/bin/time -v` with a `##PERF##` wall+maxrss line (#131 — the instrumentation #256 wished its sibling had when the 900 s run died with an unmeasured SIGKILL), compact tail block for cheap log fetches.

`docs/benchmarks.md` now opens with the two-regime table and the comparability rule — **a number is only comparable within its regime** — and everything below it is unchanged MANET content; the machine-updated results table is untouched.

Link check clean over both edited pages · workflow YAML parses · `make test` 24/24 (docs + workflow only, no protocol code).

items.title: perf(benchmark): delete the edit scenario's rows as one set on XLibur 0.300.0
items.body:
XLibur 0.300.0 added a batched whole-set row delete behind the existing `IXLRows.Delete()`: the
set collapses into a single `XLRowDeletionMap`, every formula is re-pointed against it in one
pass, and only then are the rows removed run by run with the per-run formula pass switched off.
The edit benchmark's bottom-up `ws.Row(n).Delete()` loop ran that whole-workbook formula pass 166
times and never reached the new path.

Both edit benchmarks now hand over the whole set:

```csharp
ws.Rows(EditData.RowsToDeleteSpec).Delete();   // "4,7,10,…", built once at type init
```

ClosedXML gets the identical call site rather than keeping the loop. It has the same API, and its
implementation groups by sheet and deletes bottom-up internally — exactly what the loop spelled
out by hand. So the two benchmarks stay the same line of code and what differs in the results
table is the engine, not the call. `ws.Rows(string)` is the only public route to a scattered
`IXLRows` (`XLRows` is internal, and there is no `IEnumerable<int>` overload), hence the
comma-separated form on `EditData`.

## Results

`EditAndRecalculate`, tuned counts, IronXL replayed from `snapshots/`:

| Library | Mean before | Mean after | Allocated before | Allocated after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| XLibur | 172.699 ms | **25.767 ms** | 164.91 MB | **4.39 MB** |
| ClosedXML | 351.020 ms | 358.363 ms | 337.93 MB | 337.78 MB |

ClosedXML is the control: same call site, unchanged within noise, which is what says the
speedup is XLibur's batching rather than something about how the benchmark now asks.

## Correctness

- `dotnet run -- edit`: every library still reports `U335=-139290.1236`.
- `numbers-edited-xlibur.xlsx` diffed against `numbers-edited-closedxml.xlsx`: 335 rows both,
  **zero** `SUM` range differences, identical style-group (bold row) pattern. The batched path
  fixes up references and carries the bold rows exactly like the per-row path.
- `XLRowBatchDelete.CanBatch` falls back to the per-run path for workbooks holding array,
  data-table or dynamic-array formulas. This one holds none, so the batch path is genuinely what
  is being measured.

## Notes for review

- **XLibur's row is noisy.** Error is ±16.6 ms on a 25.8 ms mean — the operation is now fast
  enough that the tuned 1–3 warmup / 5–10 iteration counts no longer settle it. The ranking sits
  far outside that interval, but the mean is not publication-tight. `-FullFidelity` (~20–25 min
  against 8m09s) would tighten it if that matters before merge.
- Read numbers here are the 50,000-row set from `main`; the branch is rebased on the PR #13 merge.
- `docs/charts.html` is regenerated locally because the `docs charts` workflow only fires on
  pushes to `main` — it will find the page unchanged on merge.
- README and `docs/index.md` libraries tables updated to 0.300.0; `update-libraries.ps1` only
  touches the csproj.

- All **6 cells reached the correct diagnosis** (`expected_outcome_matched: true`).

## What the data actually shows (read plainly, not spun)

- Raw Gradle execution time, isolated from `kmp-test`'s own wrapper overhead, did **not** favor `kmp-test-json` in this sample — if anything the opposite, consistently across both projects. This benchmark does **not** support a "`kmp-test-json` is faster" claim.
- Command count was a wash (tied in 2 of 3 scenario pairs).

Per the brief's own explicit instruction, this was not forced into the benchmark; the scenario was swapped to a small non-flaky module (`core:common`) instead, and the flaky-failure finding is disclosed in the doc's Methodology section.
- One dispatch hit a transient connection failure mid-task (pure session infrastructure, unrelated to either condition); the partial attempt was discarded and redispatched cleanly rather than resumed with uncertain state.
- Also surfaced a **disclosed, not-yet-fixed finding**: `kmp-test describe` reports `test_tasks.unit: null` for KaMPKit's `:shared` module (reads as "no tests"), while `kmp-test parallel` correctly runs 24 real passing tests there. items.title: feat(benchmarks): standalone checkpoint benchmark suite + speed benchmarks
items.body:
## Summary

New top-level `benchmarks/` suite: evaluate any checkpoint — pretrained HF, or UniRL-saved (a raw checkpoint dir is auto-exported to a PEFT adapter via `unirl.tools.export_adapter`) — across standard benchmarks under fixed, paper-comparable protocols. Zero changes to the `unirl/` package; this is the direction settled when closing #199 (the trainer's in-loop `eval/*` is a training-time signal and cannot reproduce official benchmark numbers — the 8.68-vs-12.4 confusion in #182).

- **One ckpt × N benchmarks**: `python -m benchmarks.run -b image/geneval2,image/preference --ckpt <base> [--lora <ckpt>]`; `generate` / `score` stages can run on different machines; `--report` merges all results into markdown tables.
- **Anti-bloat layout**: all code in `benchmarks/core/` (5 small modules) + `run.py`; benchmark folders hold README + data only. Adding a benchmark = data (or fetch script) + one `BenchmarkSpec` in the registry.
- **Benchmarks**: image — GenEval2 (in-repo test split), official GenEval, DPG-Bench, preference (PartiPrompts × HPSv3/PickScore/ImageReward); text — AIME24/25, MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond; video — VBench (vendored prompt suites + official-toolkit guide).
- **Scoring** reuses the `unirl-reward-service` `/score` API where its scorer *is* the benchmark metric — the geneval/geneval2 specs ship each record's `vqa_list` / `tag`+`include` as `RewardRequest.metadata`, so no service-side `dataset_path` is needed. The geneval2 scorer must honor request metadata (RewardService-side patch prepared during GPU verification, landing there separately); since a pre-metadata scorer silently degrades to a single-question template, **the runner canary-checks the service first and refuses to score non-Soft-TIFA** (verified against both scorer generations, see Test Plan). Text grading is local (math-verify, the same grader as the trainer's `mathverify` scorer, including the `\boxed{}`-wrapped gold).
- **LoRA loading is PEFT-native** (`PeftModel.from_pretrained` + `merge_and_unload`, with an all-zero-`lora_B` loud guard): `pipe.load_lora_weights()` silently drops the exported `base_model.model.` keys on SD3-family and ignores `adapter_config.json`'s `lora_alpha` (rank=32/alpha=64 recipes would be halved).
- **Data policy**: vendored when small + redistributable (licenses verified: GenEval MIT; PartiPrompts, VBench Apache-2.0; AIME24, MATH-500 MIT), fetch scripts otherwise (DPG-Bench 7.4 MB with md5 check; AIME25 card has no license; GPQA gated + canary — all three git-ignored).
- **`speed_benchmarks/`**: a general framework-speed measurement guide (wandb `perf/*` keys + `parse_perf.py`, which turns a raw training log into median s/step and samples/GPU-hour) and `verl_omni/` with the upstream **pinned as a git submodule** (exact measured commit, no code copied), a **runnable aligned SD3.5+FlowGRPO pair** (same workload/reward/hardware on both sides), and the **first measured rows**: UniRL 45.0 s/step / 7680 samples/GPU-h vs verl-omni 111.4 / 3102.8 (SDPA-aligned) and 113.6 / 3042.2 (its FA3 default) on 1×8 H20 — with work-parity reward cross-check and full disclosures in the README.

## Related Issue

Closes #182.

## Test Plan

CPU-verifiable paths first, then the GPU pass.

- `python -m benchmarks.run --list` and `--dry-run` across all specs; prompt counts match upstream exactly (553 / 800 / 1065 / 1632 / 30 / 30 / 500 / 198-gated).
- Text score stage end-to-end on synthetic completions: hand-computed acc 0.3000 reproduced; `--report` renders the table.
- `RewardServiceClient` exercised against a schema-faithful local HTTP stub (chunk boundaries, partial per-reward errors, unserved-reward rejection) mirroring `unirl-reward-service/reward_service/schemas.py`.
- Graders unit-checked: math-verify (incl. `\left(3, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)`-style golds that mis-parse unless boxed) and MC letter extraction (`\boxed{X}` + "the correct answer is (X)").
- Fetch scripts executed for real: `dpg_bench/fetch.sh` (md5 OK, 1065 unique prompts load) and `fetch_aime2025.py` (30 deduped problems; upstream ships the same set three times).
- `parse_perf.py` on a synthetic log: median/mean/p90/samples-per-GPU-hour verified by hand.
- `SKIP=no-commit-to-branch pre-commit run` on all changed files: all hooks pass.
- An adversarial multi-agent review (5 dimensions, every finding independently verified) ran over the diff; all 16 confirmed findings are fixed and regression-tested, notably: results-tag collisions across `checkpoint-<step>` dirs (now two-component tags + a `.source` marker that fails loudly), `--shard` partitioning that could overlap/leave holes under staggered launches (now partitions the full grid before the exists-filter), text scoring silently folding missing completions in as `acc=0` (now a hard error mirroring the t2i path), the SD3 LoRA-loading no-op above, `trust_env=False` on all internal HTTP calls (repo convention), and atomic PNG/torn-jsonl handling for killed runs.

**GPU verification (1×8 H20, 2026-07-14; subsets via `--num-prompts` — protocol constants untouched):**

- **t2i generate**: SD3.5-medium × {geneval2 12·k4, geneval 12·k4 **sharded `--shard 0/2`+`1/2`** (disk shows a disjoint, complete 48-image grid), preference 24·k1, dpg_bench 6·k4}; plus **FLUX.2-klein-4B** and **Z-Image-Turbo** × geneval2 (AutoPipeline coverage beyond the SD3 family). 7.1–7.2 s/img @1024²; resume short-circuit and atomic PNG publish exercised.
- **Reward-service scoring e2e** (self-deployed: geneval2 TP1 Qwen3-VL-8B + hpsv3 + pickscore + imagereward on 4 GPUs): `geneval2/vqascore` = 0.9359 (SD3.5) / 0.9066 (SD3.5 + 3-rollout LoRA) / 0.9210 (FLUX.2-klein) / 0.9162 (Z-Image-Turbo); preference = hpsv3 5.326 / pickscore 0.7901 / imagereward 0.0856; `n_errors=0` everywhere; `--report` renders the merged tables.
- **Soft-TIFA-via-metadata proven by control probe**: a deliberately false vqa question injected via request metadata scores 0.500 (mean of true+false) vs 1.0 without metadata — the scorer consumed the per-request vqa_list. The new canary guard was exercised on both paths e2e: against the **unpatched** scorer the false canary question scored 1.0000 and the runner refused with the actionable message (exit 1, nothing overwritten); against the **patched** scorer it proceeds and scores normally.
- **UniRL-ckpt → LoRA path**: 3-rollout FlowDPPO smoke (`+save_interval=3` → `checkpoint-3/checkpoint.pt`, 113 MB) → `--lora <raw-ckpt-dir>` auto-export (382 LoRA tensors + `.source` marker) → PEFT load + merge. All 48 same-seed images differ pixel-wise from base (adapter provably applied — the silent-drop failure mode excluded); merged throughput identical to base (7.1 s/img).
- **text**: vLLM-served Qwen3-8B (native 40960 ctx); math500 8×2 + aime24/25 4×2 — generate on the GPU box, **score on a different machine** (math-verify over the shared FS): acc 1.0 subsets. A first aime attempt behind `--max-model-len 32768` 400'd every request (prompt + 32768 > ctx): surfaced as per-request FAILED + hard error at score (no silent acc deflation); the aime README now documents the serving-context requirement.
- **speed_benchmarks**: pinned SD3.5+FlowGRPO pair, `sd3_vllmomni.yaml` all-default hyperparams (48 prompts × 16 samples/prompt, 10 denoise steps @512², PickScore, 2 updates/rollout), 25 rollouts on 1×8 H20. `parse_perf.py` on the real console log (`--skip 2`): **22 steady-state steps, median 94.0 s/step (mean 93.8, p90 95.0), 8.17 samples/s → 3676.6 samples/GPU-h**; engine cold-start→first rollout ≈ 6.9 min. Regex additionally validated on a trainside FlowDPPO log (11.5 s/step; samples/GPU-h hand-checked). **verl-omni side subsequently run for real** (source bring-up at its `01c87ee`, now the submodule pin): at the aligned 48×16@384² 10-step PickScore workload, UniRL 45.0 s/step / 7680.0 samples/GPU-h vs verl-omni 111.4 / 3102.8 (SDPA-aligned) and 113.6 / 3042.2 (FA3 default) — 2.48× e2e; all three runs reach the same PickScore after 25 steps (work parity). Full fairness sheet, per-phase breakdown, and engine-pin disclosures in `speed_benchmarks/verl_omni/README.md`.
- **Found + fixed during the GPU pass** (in this PR): the geneval2 canary guard above; aime serving-context README; DPG 2×2 tiling snippet (p → `item_id` mapping verified against the CSV); distilled/turbo pipeline-defaults note (Z-Image-Turbo measured 49 s/img on base-schedule defaults). Upstream **RewardService** patches prepared separately: geneval2 request-metadata support; `envs/hpsv3.txt` missing `tensorboard` + `trl==0.8.6` pins.
- **Not run**: GPQA end-to-end (gated dataset; no HF token on the boxes — fetch script + grader remain unit-tested), official-GenEval mmdet scoring and DPG mPLUG scoring (external scorers per their READMEs; generation + layout mapping verified), video/vbench generation (official-toolkit protocol; the runner does not drive video models).

## Compatibility / Risk

- Purely additive; no `unirl/` code changes. `benchmarks/` is not packaged (setuptools include stays `unirl*`).
- `.pre-commit-config.yaml`: `benchmarks/*/*/data/` joins the byte-pristine exclusions so vendored prompt sets keep verifiable upstream checksums.
- `.gitignore`: fetched/gated data and `benchmarks_results/` can never be committed.

The extension contract (new modalities = one driver; bespoke benchmarks = per-benchmark dotpath hooks when first needed; agent-style suites = wrap the official harness) is recorded at the bottom of `benchmarks/README.md`.

items.title: Add CI, contributor docs, and the project files the repo was claiming
items.body:
## What and why

An audit of engineering hygiene against this repo found four real gaps. One of them I created.

### There was no CI

Every "the gate is green" claim in this repo rested on a local run nobody else could verify. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` now runs on Python 3.11/3.12/3.13 — pytest, `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` — plus two jobs specific to this being a *benchmark* rather than a library:

- **`dataset-is-reproducible`** regenerates `data/` and fails if it differs from what's committed. Without it, someone could hand-edit an item and no test would notice — and published results would stop being traceable to the code that produced them.
- **`shortcut-audit`** runs the probe as its own job, so per-family leakage numbers are visible in the run log rather than only asserted inside the suite.

### `docs/METRICS.md` was missing Round 4 entirely

Base-rate reweighting is the most decision-relevant number the benchmark produces, and I updated README.md and DATASET.md while missing the canonical metrics reference. Now documents base rate (including why hard violations are never reweighted), the skyline (a ceiling, explicitly not a baseline), and the shortcut audit.

### No contributor docs

`CONTRIBUTING.md` leads with the **permutation rule**, because that's the invariant the whole benchmark rests on and the one a new scenario family is most likely to break. It lists the standing invariants and states plainly that a PR loosening a threshold to go green will be sent back. It also carries the two honesty rules: never publish a number you didn't produce, and when you add a capability, move its limitation out of the README.

### A license the repo claimed but didn't ship

The README has advertised a CC BY 4.0 dataset since the first commit with no such file present. `LICENSE-DATA` adds it.

Also: `CHANGELOG.md`, a PR template whose checklist covers the audit and the no-unproduced-numbers rule, and README badges so CI status is visible rather than asserted.

## Note on the commits

Formatting is deliberately its own commit (`97206bf`), separate from logic, so the reformat diff never has to be read alongside a behavior change and `git blame` points at the commit that actually wrote each line. It's verified behavior-free: 60 tests pass and the leaderboard numbers are byte-identical before and after.

This is also the first change here to go through a branch and a PR. The previous five commits went straight to `main`, which was the largest hygiene failure of the lot.

## Description
First slice of **PR #9 (Benchmarking & Scaling)**: the offline metrics/reporting scaffold. Adds an `omvqvae.benchmark` package that trains tiny `OmicsVQVAE` models under several likelihood / codebook configs on shared data and emits a comparison table of reconstruction quality, codebook utilization, and downstream separability. ## Type of change

- [x] Documentation update

## Implementation
### Changes made:
- `src/omvqvae/benchmark/metrics.py` — pure, dependency-light (NumPy/Torch-only) metrics: `codebook_usage` (dataset-level per-level perplexity + utilization = the collapse signal), `separability_score` (nearest-centroid resubstitution accuracy of the latent vs known labels = downstream-separability proxy), and `reconstruction_metrics` (mean per-cell NLL + expected-vs-target MAE in the head's native space, run in `eval`+`no_grad`).
- `src/omvqvae/benchmark/harness.py` — `BenchmarkConfig` / `BenchmarkResult`, `evaluate_model`, `run_benchmark` / `run_suite` (build model from config → `omvqvae.train.train` over an injected re-iterable `Minibatch` source → evaluate on held-out counts/labels; seeded for reproducibility), and `format_results_table` / `results_to_dicts` (Markdown table / CSV rows).

- **Pure metrics / thin harness split** so every number is unit-testable offline, matching the existing functional layering; the data source is injected (a `DataLoader` now, a Census stream later) so the same harness scales without a rewrite.
- **Reuse, don't re-implement** — `inference.encode` provides the codes+latent and `OmicsVQVAE.decode_codes` the MAE reconstruction; the harness runs `omvqvae.train.train` per config.

items.title: docs(#55): reconcile FP-count discrepancy, re-benchmark int8 vs fp32
items.body:
## Summary

Reconciles a headline-number discrepancy on baseline_v5's 303-sample test-set precision/FP count, and re-benchmarks ONNX INT8 vs FP32 quality + latency against the currently-deployed checkpoint.

**Root cause (not a bug — two things at once):**
1. The committed `experiments/baseline_v5/evaluation/test_results.json` (source of the README's "1 FN, 6 FP") predates a same-session regeneration of `data/splits/test/` — file timestamps show the checkpoint was written 21:26, that eval ran 21:43, then the test-split WAVs were rewritten 21:56 (same 21 recordings, same seed=42, same 42-FC/261-NFC composition — confirmed via `split_report.md`). It scored a since-replaced version of the split.
2. Issue #55's "4 FP / 91.1% precision" is real, but it's the **ONNX INT8** export's number, not the AST/PyTorch checkpoint's.

**Fresh, reproducible numbers** against `checkpoint-best` + the current 303-sample split (deterministic `crop_mode="center"`, reproduced twice each):

| Config | Accuracy | Precision | Recall | F1 | ROC-AUC | Confusion (TN/FP/FN/TP) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AST / PyTorch fp32 | 98.02% | 89.13% | 97.62% | 0.932 | 0.9979 | 256/5/1/41 |
| ONNX fp32 | 98.02% | 89.13% | 97.62% | 0.932 | 0.9979 | 256/5/1/41 (exact match — expected) |
| ONNX int8 | 98.35% | 91.11% | 97.62% | 0.943 | 0.9976 | 257/4/1/41 |

INT8 quantization did **not** cost precision here — it came out marginally *ahead* of fp32 (4 FP vs 5). Quantization-noise-sized on one run, not a general guarantee, but a real finding that corrects the old "no measurable quality loss" framing.

Latency (this Mac, `scripts/benchmark_platforms.py`, dummy 10s audio, p50 of 30 runs): PyTorch/MPS 56ms, ONNX fp32 429ms, ONNX int8 216ms — int8 ~2x faster.

## Changes

items.title: feat(test-runner): benchmark perf counters, metric catalog, and live results tables (I/O-bench M1–M3)
items.body:
The **benchmark measurement arc** for `sparkles:test-runner` (#85, now merged): hardware counters, a filterable metric catalog, machine-readable baselines, runtime test skipping, and a live results-table UX — 91 commits, each green on its own.

## Measurement foundation (I/O-bench harness M1–M3)

- **`--perf`** — pure-D `perf_event` hardware counters (`perf.d`, no ImportC): IPC, instructions/iter, branch/cache miss rates. A separate counting pass brackets only the timed body, so counter ioctls never perturb the ns/iter numbers; LLC-pair drop + calibration avoids PMU multiplexing.
- **M1 — metric catalog** (`metrics.d`): every measured column is a named `MetricDescriptor` tagged `MetricClass{quantitative,diagnostic}`. `--metrics=LIST` (comma / `*`-glob / `all` / `?`) picks columns and auto-opens the passes they need; `--list-metrics` prints the catalog. All unit/format semantics sit behind one `scaled`/`fixed` seam (localizes a future `sparkles.quantities` swap). Client metric names that shadow built-ins get a `user.` prefix.
- **M2 — Tier-0** (`tier0.d`): privilege-free I/O signal — `getrusage` + `/proc/self/io` per-iteration deltas (`syscr`, faults, ctx-switches, `rchar` vs `read_bytes` → cache-hit rate), with the snapshot's own cost calibrated at open and subtracted.
- **M3 — `--syscalls[=LIST]`** (`syscalls.d`): in-process `strace -c` via `perf_event_open` tracepoints — a total column plus one per named syscall.
- **`benchCase`** — matrix benchmarks: one `@benchmark` body registers a case per (engine, dataset, …) combination, each with `labels` and client throughput/level `Metric`s; failures (soft `Expected` errors, hard throws, registration-time throws) isolate into single error rows while the rest of the matrix measures. `libs/wired/bench` runs on this instead of a bespoke app.

Every backend mirrors `perf.d` (`tryOpen`/`available`/`status`/`close`/`count`, Linux + stub) and **degrades, never fails** — unavailable counters emit a stderr note and em-dash columns.

> [!NOTE]
> `--syscalls` is tracefs-root-gated on most systems: the tracepoint `id` files under `/sys/kernel/tracing` are `0700 root`, so non-root runs degrade to unavailable even when `perf_event_paranoid` allows counting. The status message and docs say so; the roadmap keeps a ptrace backend in view.

## Correctness hardening

Two adversarial review rounds (59 verified findings, all fixed). The ones that changed numbers:

- perf multiplex scaling now uses per-pass `enabled`/`running` **deltas** (`PERF_EVENT_IOC_RESET` zeroes counts but not the time fields — the cumulative ratio drifted up to −98 % under PMU contention); a never-scheduled group reports `nan`, not zeros.
- per-call timing runs on raw `MonoTime` ticks (`Duration`'s hnsecs quantized sub-100 ns samples).
- `recycledInstance` now honors over-alignment: DMD caps `align(N)` on TLS statics at 16, so the old `static T` slot was aligned only by layout luck — over-aligned slots are carved from an oversized thread-local buffer, keyed per type.

## Runner UX & CLI

- **`skipTest(reason)`** (`skip.d`, `@safe pure nothrow @nogc`): environment-gated tests skip visibly — a yellow `⊘` line + `N skipped` summary — instead of silently passing via early `return`; a skip never fails the run (exit 0). Counted correctly on every execution path, including the live parallel run.
- **`--bench-json=FILE`** — deterministic `{schema, meta, columns, rows}` document (host/compiler/knobs meta; rows in measurement order incl. error rows) for committed baseline snapshots. **`--bench-min-time=MS`** overrides the 5 ms per-case budget.
- **`--group-by=KEYS`** / **`--sort-by=KEY`** — one streamed table per label-key group / metric-column ordering (error rows always sort last).
- Hardened CLI: guarded getopt (readable errors, no raw stack traces), run-mode exclusivity, unknown `--metrics`/`--sort-by` selectors warn instead of vanishing.

## Presentation: the live results table

Adopted from the `core-cli` TUI suite (merged via #85's follow-ups on `main`):

- Timing and metric columns align on the **decimal point** (`391.00ns` over `1.5µs` compare at a glance); consecutive streamed tables share their column geometry (floors only widen during a run).
- Grouped tables carry the group name **in the top border** — the old two-row header band (and its whole span-grid layer) is gone:

  ```
  ╭──╼ benchmark: twitter/parse ╾─────────────┬────────┬─────────┬────────╮
  │ implementation │      iters │ median/iter │   ±dev │     min │    max │

## Summary

- Express the optimized MA-QAOA $p=1$ circuit in **Guppy**, compile to **HUGR**, and execute on **Quantinuum Nexus** (Selene emulator, 5000 shots). Idealized and Nexus ratios both reach **$r \approx 0.987$**.

- Add **LICENSE** + **`.gitignore`**; drop obsolete WS-QAOA test and tracked bytecode cache.

## Motivation

The previous pipeline built a circuit conceptually but did not close the loop on real Quantinuum execution infrastructure. This PR completes the hybrid story honestly: local MA-QAOA optimization, faithful Guppy re-expression, Nexus shot-based validation, and clearer documentation of what Selene does and does not prove.

## Key results

| Execution | Cut value | Ratio $r$ |
|---|---|---|
| MA-QAOA idealized (NumPy statevector) | 35.139 | 0.987 |
| MA-QAOA on Nexus (Selene, 5000 shots) | 35.130 | 0.987 |

**Idealized best-of-10:** $p=1$ → 0.987 · $p=2$ → 0.997 · $p=3$ → 1.000  
**$p=1$ mean ± std:** $0.905 \pm 0.065$

## Commits

1. `chore:` LICENSE, `.gitignore`, remove obsolete artifacts  
2. `perf:` vectorize MA-QAOA statevector and expectation evaluation  
3. `feat:` Guppy MA-QAOA circuit + Quantinuum Nexus execution

2. **`run_on_nexus.py`** — upload → execute job → measurement counts (requires prior `qnx.login()`).

Two scripts that existed only in a gitignored results directory, plus the operational knowledge from the officeqa pass that the runbook did not carry. No new document — `skills/run-benchmark/SKILL.md` and `CONFIGURATION.md` already cover most of this well, so this updates them rather than adding a competing runbook. ## Tooling, now tracked - **`scripts/launch_cell.sh`** — starts one cell detached (double-fork; macOS has no `setsid(1)` and a plain `nohup &` gets reaped), and **fails non-zero unless a live pid appears**. It had been written, lost with `runs/`, and rewritten twice. - **`scripts/wandb_progress.py`** — the only mid-run view of whether an optimizer is evaluating anything. `agent/` and `verifier/` artifacts are written only when a run *ends*, and `run.log` holds nothing but the outer spinner. ## Runbook additions **Concurrency** — it said nothing about this. Steer on the marginal error rate imposed on runs *already in flight*, not on tokens-per-minute against a published quota. That arithmetic was attempted twice on one pass and mispredicted in both directions. Measured: 4 cells at 0.15%; a fifth took the pass to 23.1% and put **17.1% on the four incumbents**. **Stopping is two operations** — killing the local process does not stop the work. Sandboxes are server-side and keep billing, so a kill converts expensive useful work into expensive useless work. Bulk cleanup mid-pass destroys healthy runs alongside orphans; run it only between passes. **Auditing a finished pass** — a degraded run still emits a plausible in-range number that sorts into your results table and does not announce itself. The five checks that make a reward a measurement are now written down, along with the fact that both audit scripts glob relative to the working directory and print an empty table from the wrong one — which reads as "no results yet" rather than "wrong directory". **Liveness traps** — `ps aux | grep` truncates its command column and reports 0 processes for perfectly healthy runs; under a kill-on-failure policy that false negative is an instruction to destroy them. items.title: feat(submission): verify the competition king record's integrity (anti-cheat on best_composite_score)
items.body:
## What does this PR do?

`leaderboard.json` carries **two** state trees. `verify_leaderboard` hardened the per-benchmark `benchmarks.*` frontier — but never touched **`competition`**, the authoritative single-king record `pr_eval._update_leaderboard` writes and whose **`best_composite_score` every APPROVE/REJECT is compared against** (`pr_eval` decides the whole contest on that one field, `pr_eval.py:634-641`).

It had **zero** integrity checking: an edited `competition.best_composite_score = 0.99` locks out every honest challenger while `verify_leaderboard` still returns `[]` ("clean"). `docs/CI.md` lists `leaderboard.json` as a sensitive path, so this is a real anti-cheat hole — the single most security-sensitive field in the file was unverified.

## How

Adds `_verify_competition` (called from `verify_leaderboard`), every invariant grounded in the writer:

- `best_composite_score` / `best_per_benchmark` / baselines / `win_margin` in `[0, 1]`;
- **`best_composite_score == mean(best_per_benchmark)`** — the composite rule (`pr_eval` sets composite = mean of the per-benchmark scores) — catches an inflated composite that doesn't match its own per-benchmark row;
- `best_composite_score == max history score`, and `best_miner`/`generation`/`pr` match the winning `history` entry (pointer consistency, mirroring the per-benchmark check);
- history entries: required fields, `merged=true`, score in `[0,1]`, non-decreasing timestamps;
- **each successive crowned king clears the previous by ≥ `win_margin`** (the APPROVE rule, `pr_eval.py:641`) — a genuinely new invariant the per-benchmark tree can't express;
- cross-subtree: every crowned win has a recorded rate-limit attempt under `benchmarks.composite` (a truncated ledger = rate-limit bypass).

It **reuses** the existing `gates.parse_utc_timestamp` / `_in_unit` / `_HISTORY_FIELDS` so it can't drift from the gate that trusts the file, folds `competition.history` timestamps into the stale-`updated_at` check, and **skips silently when `competition` is absent** so benchmarks-only leaderboards (older fixtures / partial records) stay clean.

## Scope

Read-only; the **committed `leaderboard.json` verifies clean** (no false positive). New `tests/test_leaderboard_competition_verify.py` (19 offline cases): the inflated-composite anti-cheat, composite-vs-history mismatch, pointer tampering, an illegal sub-margin crowning, non-merged/backwards-timestamp history, the rate-limit-bypass cross-check, and robustness (non-dict / non-list `competition`). The tamper cases **fail on `main`** (which ignores `competition` entirely) and pass here.

- Pure python — **no torch, no network**. `ruff` + `mypy` clean; the full leaderboard suite (63 tests) is green.

## Duplication note

Not an Rn invariant verifier and unrelated to the oracle-ceiling / results_table / DoD work in the other open PRs — this is `submission/`-side integrity of the `competition` object, which no open PR touches.

## Summary

Migrates model persistence to native Keras `.keras` save/load, fixes a cluster of bugs that left the documented `job="train_prediction"` flow completely broken, adds a reproducible benchmark suite comparing the CLV pipeline against a naive baseline, and cleans up dependency pinning and docs. Version bumped `0.1.9` → `0.4`.

## What's included

**Model persistence rework**
- Replaced JSON-config + separate-weights save/load with native Keras `.keras` format across all three models (removed `model_from_to_json`)
- Updated model filename path handling

**Dependency fixes** (`pyproject.toml`)
- `tensorflow`: `^2.18.0` → `>=2.18.0,<2.20.0` — TF ≥2.20 has a protobuf symbol clash with pyarrow that crashes on import on macOS ARM
- `python`: `^3.11` → `>=3.11,<3.13` — avoids resolving to a Python version TensorFlow has no wheels for

**Bug fixes in the train/predict pipeline** (found while building the benchmark — the documented `job="train_prediction"` path had never been exercised end-to-end; no tests existed to catch it)
- `next_purchase_model.py` / `next_purchase_prediction.py`: missing call to write the prediction input file; swapped `temp_data_path`/`directory` arguments; `future_date` collapsed to 0-day horizon; results written to a path the merge step never reads from
- `newcomers.py` / `purchase_amount_model.py`: `Adam(lr=...)` → `learning_rate=...` (Keras 3 rename); dead code path calling a method with a missing required arg; `to_dict("results")` → `to_dict("records")` (invalid pandas orient); `layers.LSTM(batch_size=...)` — unsupported kwarg in Keras 3
- `functions.py`: missing import of `accepted_ratio_of_actual_order` used in a pandas query string; `filters` hyperparameter incorrectly float-cast instead of int, breaking `Conv1D` during hyperparameter tuning

**New benchmark suite** (`benchmark/`)
- Synthetic transaction generator (400 customers, 4 segments), naive CLV baseline (AOV × frequency × horizon), hand-rolled MAE/RMSE/SMAPE metrics, and an orchestrator comparing baseline vs. CLV with default params vs. CLV with real hyperparameter tuning
- Results: CLV model portfolio-level total error is 8-20% vs. 319% for the naive baseline; naive baseline is still more accurate per-customer on this dataset size — see `docs/benchmark.md`

**Docs & README**
- New `docs/benchmark.md`, wired into `mkdocs.yml` nav
- Typo/grammar cleanup across all `docs/*.md` pages; corrected stale `.json`/`.h5` model-format references to `.keras`
- README rebuilt with a How It Works section, benchmark results table, dashboard screenshots, quick start example, and a docs index table

## What

The engine's internals already describe scheduling in exactly these terms — `interp.rs` calls `(layer, index)` "a valid topological order", with `layer[i]` the longest path to `i` over all upstream edges, and the work set draining in ascending order. The user-facing docs were the only place still calling it *breadth-first*, and the comparison against reactive/async frameworks the only place calling those *depth-first*.

This reterms the next tree: wingfoil is **topologically sorted**; the frameworks it is measured against **propagate one path at a time** (*per-path*). Two directories follow the wording:

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| `examples/core/breadth_first/` | `examples/core/topological_sort/` |
| `benches/bfs_vs_dfs/` | `benches/topological_vs_per_path/` |

Prose updated in the root README, `examples/README.md`, `examples/core/README.md`, the `ema_crossover` / `odds_evens` / `fanout_10x10` / `async` example READMEs, `async/main.rs`, `src/lib.rs`, `benches/README.md`, the three bench headers, `plot.py`, the rxrust dev-dependency comment, `scripts/bench-report.sh`, and two lines in `docs/port-plan.md`.

Per the rule in `CLAUDE.md` — target names are decoupled from directory names and must not change. `cargo run --example breadth_first` and the three `bfs_vs_dfs_*` benches keep working exactly as before. This branch was rebased onto #662, which captured a real measured reading while it was out. That reading is where most of the remaining vocabulary lived, so it is covered here too:

- the `## Breadth-first vs depth-first` section of `benches/README.md`, including its links into the bench directory — those would have 404'd after the rename;

items.title: Narrow benchmark runs on pull requests to changed code
items.body:
## Summary

This change implements intelligent scoping for benchmark runs on pull requests. Instead of running the full benchmark suite (21 jobs measuring all indexers across all scenarios), pull requests now only re-run benchmarks for the indexers and scenarios that were actually changed, significantly reducing CI time while maintaining result accuracy.

## Key Changes

- **New `select-scope.ts` script**: Analyzes git diffs to determine which indexers and scenarios need to be re-measured based on what files changed. The logic handles:
  - Indexer-specific code changes (only that indexer in that scenario)
  - Scenario run logic changes (all indexers in that scenario)
  - Driver changes (affected indexer in all scenarios)
  - Shared harness/workflow changes (all indexers in all scenarios)
  - Documentation and known local-only scripts (no benchmarks needed)
  - Anything the filter does not recognize (full run — over-running only costs runner time, while under-running would publish stale rows as fresh)

- **New `test-scope.ts` script**: Comprehensive test suite for the scope selection logic, covering edge cases like the envio/envio-rpc dual-directory mapping and ensuring correct behavior across different file change patterns. Both of the filter's hardcoded maps (`INDEXER_DIRS`, `DRIVER_INDEXERS`) are pinned against the drivers registry so they cannot drift silently.

- **Updated `benchmarks.yml` workflow**:
  - Setup job now checks out the repo and runs `select-scope.ts` for pull requests (the checkout and Node setup are skipped on `main` and dispatch runs, which never diff anything)
  - Dynamically generates per-scenario indexer lists instead of using a single matrix
  - Adds `partial` flag to indicate when a run was narrowed
  - Summary job skips if no benchmark-related changes detected
  - Passes `PARTIAL_RUN` flag to result tables and PR comments
  - The PR comment calls out indexers that were selected to run but reported no result, so a real job failure cannot hide behind the "carried forward" scope note

- **Updated `build-tables.ts`**: Distinguishes between carried-forward results due to partial runs (normal for PRs) versus actual job failures, adjusting warning messages accordingly, and hands the per-case failure list to the comment step. Also warns when a failed indexer has no published row to carry forward at all.

## Implementation Details

- The scope selection uses environment variables (`CHANGED_FILES`, `ALL_CASES`, `ALL_INDEXERS`) to remain testable and shell-friendly
- Special handling for `envio-rpc` which lives in the `envio/` directory but is a separate indexer
- Shared driver modules (`common`, `index`) trigger full runs; tool-specific drivers only affect their indexer(s)
- Inert paths (docs, local test scripts, archived results) are an explicit allowlist; the default for unrecognized files is a full run
- Results maintain canonical ordering regardless of diff order for consistent matrix/table layout
- Pull requests that change nothing benchmark-related skip the entire benchmark run and summary

items.title: feat(bench, build, cli): add jq substring-search A/B benchmark + defer phase 2
items.body:
## Description

This PR completes Phase 1 of issue #303: a bench-only A/B micro-benchmark measuring `memchr::memmem` (SIMD) against Rust's std substring search (scalar Two-Way) for jq substring builtins. The benchmark systematically measures performance across haystack lengths (8 B–64 KB), needle lengths (1–64 B), and operation shapes (index, rindex, indices, contains, split), while maintaining semantic correctness through a comprehensive parity guard.

The results show memmem winning decisively in its target regime (5.9× at 64 KB, 52× for 1-byte needles) but losing on long needles and allocation-bound ops. Per the #126 decision gate requiring >40% scan share *and* a realistic large-string workload (#301), the disciplined outcome is to defer adoption. This matches seven prior codebase precedents (P2.6, P2.8, P3, P5, P8) where micro-bench wins did not translate to end-to-end improvements. The benchmark is retained as the reusable harness for Phase 2 once #301 lands.

## Type of Change
- [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality)
- [x] Test coverage improvement
- [x] Documentation update
- [x] CI/CD changes

## Related Issue
Refs #303 (follow-up to #126)  
Depends on #301 (realistic large-string workload for Phase 2 validation)

## Changes Made

**Benchmark Implementation:**
- Added `benches/jq_string_ops_bench.rs`: A/B micro-benchmark with 473 lines of Criterion harness
  - Both std and memmem variants for `index`, `rindex`, `indices`, `contains`, `split` implemented in-file
  - Std variants mirror exact `eval.rs` call shapes; `eval.rs` deliberately untouched
  - Comprehensive corpus generation with filler alphabet, needle positioning (start/middle/end), and separator frequency control
  - Eight benchmark groups covering full input matrix: haystack length sweep, needle length effect, reverse scan, predicate testing, overlapping matches, and split density
- Added `check_parity()` guard: runs before any timing, enforces byte-for-byte parity between implementations
  - Validates `indices` overlapping semantics (`indices("aaaa", "aa") == [0,1,2]`, not `[0,2]`)
  - Validates `split` empty-part edge cases (trailing/adjacent separators, empty haystack)
  - Validated on all 9 haystack sizes, needle positions, and real operation outputs

**Cargo.toml & Build:**
- Added `memchr 2.7` as dev-dependency with rationale (already transitive via serde_json; supply-chain no-op)
- Registered `[[bench]]` target `jq_string_ops_bench` with `harness = false` (allows `check_parity` to run without libtest)

**Benchmark Registry:**
- Registered `jq_string_ops_bench` in `src/bin/succinctly/bench_runner/registry.rs`
  - Category: Json
  - Type: Criterion
  - Description: "Micro: jq substring search — std vs memchr::memmem (issue #303)"

**Documentation:**
- Added `docs/optimizations/jq-string-search.md`: comprehensive Phase 1 finding document
  - Problem statement: scalar Two-Way vs SIMD on long haystacks with rare needles
  - Method: bench-only, input matrix, parity guard design, M4 Pro platform
  - Full results table: 5.9× peak at 64 KB, 52× for 1-byte needle, losses on long needles (0.76×) and short misses (0.31×)
  - Interpretation: seven-point analysis of why green micro-bench is insufficient without workload validation
  - Decision gate application: scan share <20% for allocation-bound ops; no jq benchmark or large-string corpus exists
  - Phase 2 caveats: if opened after #301, restrict to genuine substring-search ops, keep overlapping `indices`, preserve `split` empty-part semantics
  - Reproduction instructions
- Updated `docs/optimizations/README.md`: added jq-string-search row to table, added Notable Failures entry
- Updated `docs/optimizations/history.md`: added "⏸️ jq Substring Search" entry with status/problem/technique/results/insight/files

## Testing

**Automated Testing:**
- [x] All existing tests pass (zero changes to `eval.rs`)
- [x] New `check_parity()` guard enforces semantic correctness before any timing
  - Tests `indices` overlapping on 6 inputs ("aaaa", "abababab", "mississippi", etc.)
  - Tests `split` empty-part edge cases on 8 inputs (trailing sep, adjacent seps, leading sep, etc.)
  - Tests `index` / `rindex` / `contains` agreement on boundaries and misses (6 inputs)
  - Validates all 9 haystack sizes and needle positions match between std and memmem

**Manual Testing:**
- [x] Measured on Apple M4 Pro (ARM64, NEON)
- [x] Not measured on x86_64 (does not change decision, which is gated on workload existence, not micro numbers)

### Test Commands
```bash
cargo bench --bench jq_string_ops_bench   # Run A/B benchmark (executes check_parity first)
cargo test --bench jq_string_ops_bench    # Run parity guard only (harness=false)
succinctly bench run jq_string_ops_bench  # Via bench runner (requires feature: bench-runner)
```

## Performance Impact
- [x] Performance improvement (benchmark only; no production code changes)

**Benchmark Results (M4 Pro, criterion median):**
- `index` absent @ 64 KB: **5.9×** (8.4 → 49.6 GiB/s)
- `index` absent, 1-byte needle @ 16 KB: **52×** (2.1 → 108.9 GiB/s)
- `index` absent, 64-byte needle @ 16 KB: 0.76× (memmem loses)
- `contains` miss @ 64 B: 0.31× (memmem loses)
- `split` dense sep / `indices` overlapping: 1.1–1.5× (allocation-bound, scan is minority)

**Production Impact**: None. Zero changes to `src/jq/eval.rs` or runtime code. This is Phase 1 measurement only.

## Checklist
- [x] My code follows the project's style guidelines
- [x] I have performed a self-review of my code
- [x] I have added comprehensive parity tests via `check_parity()`
- [x] New and existing tests pass locally
- [x] I have updated documentation (jq-string-search.md, README, history)
- [x] My changes generate no new warnings
- [x] Benchmark harness validates semantic correctness before timing
- [x] eval.rs remains untouched (zero production risk)

## Additional Notes

**Why This Is Phase 1 Measurement, Not Phase 2 Implementation:**

Per the #126 decision gate:
- ✓ Micro-benchmark complete: memmem wins in target regime (5.9–52×)
- ✗ Scan share >40%: allocation-bound ops collapse to 1.1–1.5×; scan is minority of wall-time
- ✗ Realistic large-string workload: #301 does not yet exist; no jq benchmark exercises these ops
- Result: Reject/defer, matching seven prior codebase precedents (P2.6, P2.8, P3, P5, P8)

**Semantics Preserved (Guarded by `check_parity`):**
- `indices` is overlapping: `indices("aaaa", "aa") → [0,1,2]`, not `[0,2]`
- `split` empty parts: trailing sep yields trailing `""`; adjacent seps yield interior `""`
- Both enforced before any timing, on all corpus variants

**Bench-Only Risk Assessment**: Zero production risk. `eval.rs` untouched. All changes are:
- Benchmark harness (benches/jq_string_ops_bench.rs)
- Build configuration (Cargo.toml, registry.rs)
- Documentation (docs/optimizations/)

**Forward Path**: Retain `benches/jq_string_ops_bench.rs` as the reusable harness. When #301 delivers a realistic large-single-string workload and validates that scan share exceeds 40% end-to-end, Phase 2 can adopt memmem respecting the caveats documented in jq-string-search.md.

found this again mid-Stage-3C when a representative embedded regression
check for `placement-inspector-workflows` was still in its first part after
